newsitem.title: GERMANY: Receding floods leave behind more united Germany.
newsitem.headline: Receding floods leave behind more united Germany.

text.p: A titanic struggle to stave off massive floods has brought Germans closer together than at any time since the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
The threat of Germany's worst postwar natural disaster sparked a show of solidarity between east and west, doing much to erode what people here call the wall that remains in the minds of Germans.

For nearly three weeks, thousands of soldiers and aid workers from all corners of the country have toiled on the banks of the River Oder in eastern Germany in a spectacular display of muscle and machine.

Working side by side on the muddy dikes, they piled tonnes of sandbags to hold back the waters. In millions of homes throughout the country, blanket television coverage showed scenes of east German families who had lost new homes and tenacious farmers who had lived through Hitler's Third Reich and 40 years of communism.

Members of the public have donated millions to aid flood victims. During a benefit programme on ARD public television on Sunday, more than four million marks ($2.1 million) were donated and Germany's largest company Daimler-Benz AG pledged one million marks.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, with a keen sense for public opinion, saw that not only the first fruits of German unity were at stake, but the very future of his greatest political achievement, as east and west were called upon to join together.

"This is where we have to prove that unified Germany is one Fatherland," Kohl said during a vist to the Oder last week at the height of tension, when it seemed the river would burst its banks at any moment, submerging dozens of villages.

The floods began receding at the weekend and Brandenburg state officials are now increasingly optimistic that the water-logged dikes will hold long enough to allow the river to fall below the danger point over the next few days.

Hundreds of homes were flooded to the rooftops in Wiesenau, Ziltendorf and Brieskow-Finkenheerd, small towns south of Frankfurt an der Oder, a city of 18,000 that is linked to Slubice in Poland by the "Bridge of Peace".
Germany escaped the worst of catastrophic flooding in central Europe caused by torrential rains that killed over 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic last month.

But a break in the Oder dikes, particularly in the vulnerable line of flood walls along the Oderbruch region, would have engulfed a low-lying basin of farmland that was last flooded in 1947, when lives were lost and farms destroyed.

Kohl was quick to point out that the tragedy of 50 years ago could be prevented now because Germany was unified and wealthy westerners could send in people and technology to protect the homes and farms of their brethren in the east.

Many eastern Germans who had lived through the floods of 1947 shared Kohl's impression. Many were also aware now that German unity has brought new wealth and opportunity to the east, not just unemployment and uncertainty.

"Those of us who spent 40 years in East Germany never had it as good as those in the West," said Magdalena Schroeder, 63, of Hohenwutzen, whose village in the northern Oderbruch basin was the Achilles heel in the 70 km (45 mile) line of dikes.

"We learned how to help one another because we had to, and that is just what we are doing now. But the westerners brought their technology along with the soldiers and if they hadn't we would have been under water a long time ago," she said.

After suffering an identity crisis for 40 years as it searched for a purpose, the German army appears to have discovered itself on the banks of the Oder and for the first time to have been fully embraced by the population at large.

German newspapers for the past week have had no shortage of glossy photographs of columns of young soldiers, tired and carrying spades instead of rifles, returning from 12-hour shifts filling sandbags and reinforcing the fragile dikes.

There is no doubt in the minds of local villagers that dikes would have broken last week without the 10,000 soldiers, dozens of helicopters and heavy earth-moving equipment deployed to the region. And for many of the soldiers, it marked the first time they felt they had a purpose.

Their role was best summed up by Brandenburg's environment minister, Matthias Platzeck, who told reporters during the most critical phase of the operation, when thousands of soldiers toiled through the night: "This gives entirely new meaning to the term 'defending your country'."
($ = 1.863 German Marks)
